Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette: Ahmed, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern man, recently divorced and working as a tax inspector in Los Angeles, has been struggling with profound distress following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The event itself was seared into his memory: he had been driving home from work when another car, likely impaired by alcohol, veered into his lane and collided head-on with his vehicle. Ahmed remembers the smell of burning rubber and fuel, the screech of metal grinding against metal, and the overwhelming scent of alcohol that permeated the air. The impact was so severe that it left him trapped inside his car for nearly an hour before he could be extricated by emergency personnel. Since then, Ahmed has been on a downward spiral, unable to shake off the haunting images and visceral reactions. Any sight or smell reminiscent of the crash triggers intense anxiety and panic. The sound of screeching tires or the alcohol aroma wafting from nearby bars are enough to send him into a tailspin. His response to these triggers is to escape into his phone, playing games or browsing the internet for hours on end to avoid confronting his thoughts and emotions. Ahmed had come to believe that he could not rely on himself anymore; the trauma had left him feeling incapable of doing the things that once defined him as competent and strong. This sense of helplessness has further exacerbated his coping mechanisms. He spends long hours on his phone, avoiding social interactions and even driving altogether. His hypervigilance is constant: he is superalert and jumps at unexpected or loud sounds, which only reinforces his belief that he cannot trust himself to navigate the world safely. The fear of encountering another triggering situation has led him to avoid driving entirely, severely limiting his ability to perform essential tasks required for his job as a tax inspector. Ahmed's undereating is also a manifestation of this coping strategy; he often skips meals or restricts his food intake, feeling that controlling something in his life gives him a semblance of order. However, this only deepens the cycle of negative appraisals and maladaptive behaviors. His belief that he will never feel normal emotions again leads him to further isolate himself from others, which makes it harder for him to seek support or find healthy ways to cope. The interplay between his triggers and threats is a self-reinforcing loop. Every time Ahmed encounters a car similar to the one involved in the crash or smells alcohol, he becomes hyperalert, certain that danger lurks around every corner. This hypervigilance only heightens his anxiety and reinforces the idea that he cannot trust himself to handle these situations. As a result, he retreats even further into avoidance behaviors like playing games on his phone for hours. Ahmed's work as a tax inspector has become increasingly difficult due to his inability to drive to inspections or meetings outside of his immediate office location. His colleagues have noticed his absence and the quality of his work has suffered, leading to tension with supervisors who are growing concerned about his performance. The realization that he is no longer capable of fulfilling his professional responsibilities further erodes his self-esteem and reinforces his negative appraisals. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a combination of increasing isolation, worsening anxiety attacks at the mere thought of leaving his house, and the fear that he would lose his job if things didn't improve. He is most afraid of never being able to return to his former self or feeling like a burden on others due to his struggles. At the same time, Ahmed hopes for a way to regain some sense of control over his life and find healthier coping mechanisms to deal with his trauma. Through the lens of Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model, it is evident that Ahmed's core negative appraisals are driving both his maladaptive strategies and heightened threat monitoring. His triggers, while potent, are also part of a broader cycle where each component fuels the other in a relentless feedback loop. Seeking help represents a critical step for Ahmed to break this cycle and regain some semblance of control over his life.
